title: SQL vs NoSQL
description: Compare SQL and NoSQL databases to understand when to use relational versus document, key-value, or graph stores in system design.

data.text: Choosing between SQL and NoSQL is one of the first and most consequential database decisions in any system design interview. SQL databases use structured tables with predefined schemas, while NoSQL databases trade schema rigidity for flexibility and scale. Understanding their strengths and trade-offs determines whether your design will handle the workload reliably.

SQL databases like PostgreSQL and MySQL organize data into rows and columns with a strict schema. They enforce ACID properties—Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability—ensuring reliable transactions even during failures. SQL excels when relationships between entities matter: orders tied to customers, products linked to categories, or comments tied to users.

data.text: NoSQL databases come in four main types: document stores like MongoDB, key-value stores like Redis, wide-column stores like Cassandra, and graph databases like Neo4j. They generally prioritize horizontal scaling and flexible schemas over strict consistency guarantees. NoSQL shines when data is semi-structured, write throughput is extreme, or the data model naturally fits a non-relational pattern.

data.title: When to choose NoSQL
data.text: Choose NoSQL when you need massive write throughput, flexible schemas for evolving product requirements, or natural data access patterns that don't map well to joins.

Start with SQL unless you have a specific reason to choose NoSQL. Most applications involve relationships, transactions, or reporting queries that SQL handles elegantly. Choose NoSQL when you need sub-second writes at massive scale, when your data model is inherently nested or graph-like, or when you must support offline-first mobile sync.

items.question: Can I use both SQL and NoSQL in one system?
items.answer: Yes. Many production systems use SQL for transactional data and NoSQL for specific high-throughput or flexible-schema needs. This hybrid approach is common in practice.

items.question: Does NoSQL mean no joins at all?
items.answer: Most NoSQL databases don't support server-side joins, but you can denormalize data or perform application-side joins. Graph databases like Neo4j are an exception and handle relationships natively.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: SQL databases enforce strict schemas and ACID transactions, making them ideal for relational, transaction-heavy workloads.
NoSQL databases trade schema rigidity for horizontal scale and flexibility, excelling at massive write throughput and evolving data models.
Start with SQL and add NoSQL only when a specific scaling or flexibility requirement justifies the added complexity.
